scope: Stress test of eight Latin American and African rights-enforcement proposals. Evidence cutoff 2026-10-31; Geneva checkpoint 2027-06-21/22. Assessments concern incremental evidence, not adoption or measured effects. Regulator, affected-community and startup lenses are analytical except where an original position is explicitly attributed. No scores changed.

routes.headline: Grok supplies an actual failure-to-correction evidence demand, stronger than an inspection-programme promise

newEvidence.claim: Official account: on 11 February 2026 ANPD, MPF and Senacon said X's response lacked concrete efficacy evidence and their preliminary technical tests found continuing failures. This is observed regulatory reporting, not independently replicated testing.
newEvidence.locator: Opening three paragraphs

newEvidence.claim: ANPD's preventive measure invokes inspection-regulation arts.32 III and 35, requires all versions/plans/modalities to prevent the specified nonconsensual sexualized outputs, and gives five business days for verifiable documentary evidence. The identified file is 00261.000178/2026-27 and technical note 1/2026/FIS/CGF/ANPD (0239948).
newEvidence.locator: Medidas adotadas / ANPD

newEvidence.claim: Official account: MPF demanded monthly reports; ANPD described possible escalation to daily fines and sanction proceedings. These are distinct agencies and mechanisms, not a single jointly exercised veto.
newEvidence.locator: MPF and Próximos passos

supports: Regulator lens (inference): an actual evidence request and a documented failed response reduce the authority/novelty gap for a narrowly scoped technical dossier.
Affected-person lens (inference): preventing nonconsensual sexualized depictions is a direct harm-reduction objective, not merely administrative compliance.
challenges: The proposed annex should add held-out, version-specific verification rather than claim to introduce efficacy evidence for the first time.

Startup lens (analytical, not X testimony): an all-versions demand can be expensive and technically under-specified; bound applicable interfaces, lawful synthetic test material, evidence access and the decision threshold.
The earlier long sanction-duration comparator does not measure urgent preventive-action time. Conversely, five days to respond is not five days to achieve an effective remedy.
unknowns: Current status and any later modification of the February measure; full technical note; receipt and response dates; independently verified successful retest; affected-user denominator; staff-hours.
No football-club case file was recovered in this pass. Do not represent the Grok file as a football-cohort result.
routes.decisionTest: Recover the named file's actual demand, response and subsequent technical finding. Strengthen remedy only if a versioned independent retest shows the prohibited failure materially reduced and records the action on residual failures.

ideas.title: Grok correction-evidence case audit
ideas.proposal: Use the existing identified ANPD file as the first evidence audit; compare the regulator's original failing examples with a separately constructed held-out set and an all-interface/version inventory. This is a proposed audit, not a new order or an assertion the case remains open.
ideas.owner: ANPD inspection team as legal decision owner; X as obligor; technically independent evaluator only if lawfully authorised
ideas.mechanism: Existing case-specific preventive evidence demand under inspection-regulation arts.32 III and 35; additional testing requires lawful case scope
ideas.safetyDemand: Prevent the specified nonconsensual sexualized outputs; preserve auditable evidence of correction without circulating victim images
ideas.verification: Record actual order and receipt dates, version/interface hashes, original and held-out results, false positives, evaluator access and regulator disposition. Use lawful non-abusive synthetic proxies; do not generate victim content for a public demonstration.
ideas.remedy: Regulator determines whether residual legally relevant failure warrants additional preventive directions, daily fine or sanction process; evaluator does not impose sanctions
ideas.deadline: Proposed: scope/status check by 2026-12-15, evidence audit by 2027-03-31, persistence check by 2027-06-01; original five-business-day demand is historical
dependencies: Actual case access and lawful testing authorisation
Independent evaluator capacity and confidentiality protections
Potential adverse effects: overblocking lawful expression, re-exposure of victims, shifting abuse to untested interfaces; include appeal and error checks
ideas.whyBetter: Tests an already consequential demand and known failed assurance instead of counting programme activities or voluntary policies

scoreImplications.reason: Actual case identifies an obligor, legal provisions and verifiable-evidence demand
Specific serious harm is explicit; no inference about catastrophic-risk reduction is needed
The source documents continuing failures and an order, not a successful final retest

routes.headline: An internal accountable owner is in the law, but recommendations remain nonbinding and exemptions are broad

newEvidence.claim: Re-read statute: art.77 makes each controller's Comité de Transparencia its highest personal-data authority; art.78 I, IV, V and VIII assign coordination, criteria, security-control supervision and reporting suspected irregularities to internal control.

Re-read statute: arts.68 and 72 expressly make assessment recommendations nonbinding. Article 73 also exempts cases where, in the obliged body's judgment, assessment could compromise the intended effects, as well as emergency/urgency cases.

supports: Regulator lens (inference): the committee is a concrete internal governance candidate instead of an unidentified generic public-body owner.
challenges: A data-protection committee is not automatically the software release or procurement signatory. Delegation remains to be established.
Affected-community lens: requiring evidence only from self-declared qualifying projects could miss precisely the sensitive deployments exempted under art.73.
Startup lens: duplicated committee, receiving-authority and procurement requests may add cost without a predictable hold/release decision; agree one evidence package.
unknowns: No fresh completed AI assessment or remedy case recovered; current operational receiving/signing unit and later amendments remain unverified.
No identified deployment, signed internal hold, exemption determination or effective remedy to affected people.
routes.decisionTest: Obtain one named body's committee resolution, legally delegated release decision and recorded art.73 applicability determination; demonstrate an actual privacy failure changes the deployment decision.

scoreImplications.implication: Narrow role uncertainty, not consent uncertainty
scoreImplications.reason: Arts.77–78 identify an internal owner but do not supply agreement or release delegation
Nonbinding advice and self-assessed exemptions remain material

routes.headline: Final administrative Worldcoin decision demands externally certified deletion with technical evidence

newEvidence.claim: SIC's 8 July 2026 original account says Resolution 45710 of 18 June 2026 rejected the companies' appeal and confirmed Resolution 78798 of 3 October 2025; it describes immediate permanent closure of sensitive-data processing and deletion including iris codes, with external certification and technical evidence required.
newEvidence.locator: Opening two paragraphs; concluding paragraph beginning En conclusión

newEvidence.claim: SIC reports rejecting the companies' claim that encrypted distributed SMPC/AMPC fragments ceased being personal data. It says individualisation remains the system's purpose and that the companies had not clearly explained deletion in the distributed architecture.
newEvidence.locator: El componente técnico: el cifrado y la fragmentación no eximen del cumplimiento

newEvidence.claim: The October 2025 release described the prohibition as all personal-data processing, whereas the July 2026 release describes sensitive-data processing. Do not silently equate the scopes without the dispositive orders.
newEvidence.locator: Opening and concluding operative summaries in each release

supports: Regulator lens: actual foreign obligors and technical-evidence-backed corrective obligations are identifiable, substantially stronger than a hypothetical circular pilot.
Affected-community lens: the decision addresses consent and usable habeas-data procedures, not only security of retained data.
challenges: This is a Law 1581 biometric-processing case, not evidence that Circular 002's proposed AI retest annex has been used.
Final administrative sanction is not observed deletion, no further administrative appeal is not proof that judicial review is unavailable, and the release is not the full decision.

Startup lens: cryptographic protection may reduce exposure without curing unlawful collection; do not conflate a technically strong architecture with a lawful business process. Company arguments here are reported by SIC, not independently retrieved company testimony.
unknowns: External certificate, its technical methodology and actual deletion date; all processor/nodes/backup coverage; full appeal decision; later judicial challenge; current compliance status.
No verified harmed-user count or causal reduction estimate.
routes.decisionTest: Retrieve the ordered external certificate and match every data location and iris-code derivative to the deletion scope; test residual matching and re-ingestion, and obtain SIC's acceptance or deficiency finding.

ideas.title: Prove deletion across a distributed biometric system
ideas.proposal: Use Colombia's ordered external certification as a bounded deletion-verification case, with Kenya's reported court-supervised deletion as a comparator. Keep the two countries' legal decisions separate; share only a nonpersonal evidence schema if lawful.
ideas.owner: SIC's personal-data authority as Colombian acceptance owner; World Foundation and Tools for Humanity as obligors; the external certifier required by the decision
ideas.mechanism: Resolution 45710/2026 confirming 78798/2025, as described by SIC; obtain operative text before implementing the protocol
ideas.safetyDemand: Make the ordered suppression effective across iris codes, derived representations, storage nodes and re-ingestion paths; retain a usable data-subject remedy
ideas.verification: Join asset inventory, processor attestations, backup/retention exceptions and independently witnessed deletion logs; use authorised synthetic canaries to test residual matching and re-creation. Record what cannot be verified, not just a certificate number.
ideas.remedy: SIC evaluates deficient compliance under the existing decision and applicable process; do not invent a new automatic penalty or permit restart on a laboratory pass
ideas.deadline: Proposed: obtain operative order/certificate by 2026-12-15; technical review by 2027-03-31; persistence and rights-request check by 2027-06-01
dependencies: Operative order and lawful access to certifier evidence
Technical interpretation of secret sharing and backups
Potential adverse effects: proving deletion could itself reveal sensitive linkages; deletion can destroy evidence for claimants; preserve lawful litigation records and minimise audit data
No coordination or institutional consent assumed from similarity of the two cases
ideas.whyBetter: Tests the substantive outcome behind a legally consequential certificate and detects false compliance; preserves direct rights value without claiming a frontier-model release veto

scoreImplications.reason: A final administrative order explicitly requires external certification plus technical evidence; no certificate read

scoreImplications.implication: Credit direct consent/deletion protections separately from frontier-risk speculation

routes.headline: Signed WhatsApp notice demonstrates an evidence obligation, but is not a section-57 linkage precedent

newEvidence.claim: The signed WhatsApp section-95 notice is dated 10 September 2024, although the regulator's index lists it under 16 April 2025. It orders a detailed PIIA, a risk register and implementation report within 60 days of receipt; it provides 30 days from receipt to appeal.
newEvidence.locator: Notice pp.9–11, C6, C7.1, D, E and signature; index WhatsApp entry

newEvidence.claim: The regulator rejects taking claimed safeguards on trust. The notice records WhatsApp's concern that sharing confidential security details could undermine security, but finds failure to demonstrate safeguards and orders a risk register.

supports: Regulator lens: signed evidence and PIIA obligations give a concrete enforcement analogue beyond generic guidance.
Affected-community lens: notice also addresses consent, purpose limitation and comprehensible rights information; protection is wider than disclosure testing.
challenges: The notice is section 95 enforcement, not proof that the proposed AI linkage qualifies under section 57 or has prior authorisation.

Startup lens (analytical): minimise duplicate dossiers and protect security details; the company's confidentiality objection is regulator-reported evidence, not an independently sourced startup position.
A dated order and current web listing do not prove its implementation or absence of litigation.
unknowns: Receipt date, appeal/stay status, implementation report, successful safeguards verification; a named section-57 AI linkage applicant.
Regulator litigation index read but does not resolve this case; its silence is not proof of no appeal.
routes.decisionTest: First establish both statutory linkage conditions for the actual project; separately recover the WhatsApp report and disposition as an enforcement analogue, without transferring its authority or timeline to prior authorisation.

scoreImplications.implication: Analogue supports evidence demand, not exact-route completion
scoreImplications.reason: Signed PIIA/risk-register order exists, but successful retest and section-57 applicability are unproven

scoreImplications.implication: Do not use 60 days as observed turnaround
scoreImplications.reason: Clock is a case-specific reporting requirement from unlocated receipt date

routes.headline: Litigant reports completed court-supervised deletion; this is stronger than a DPIA count but still needs technical corroboration

newEvidence.claim: Original litigant statement: Katiba Institute welcomes deletion of unlawfully collected Worldcoin data and commends ODPC for ensuring full compliance. It describes the 5 May 2025 judgment as prohibiting collection without a lawful adequate DPIA or using cryptocurrency-induced consent, and ordering deletion within seven days under ODPC supervision.
newEvidence.locator: Opening paragraph and paragraph beginning In a judgment delivered on 5 May 2025

newEvidence.claim: The Institute's own position is that privacy, dignity and data protection must constrain innovation; its Executive Director frames implementation as a response to extractive treatment of African data. This is actual civil-society advocacy, not a representative survey of affected Kenyans.
newEvidence.locator: Paragraphs 2 and final paragraph attributed to Nora Mbagathi

newEvidence.claim: A separate news reproduction hosted by Katiba dates ODPC's confirmation to 20 January 2026. That date is secondary reporting; the original ODPC notice and technical report were not recovered.
newEvidence.locator: Reprint paragraph beginning Its mandate; footer says first published by The Star; ODPC site returned maintenance page

supports: Regulator/rights lens: a public-interest litigant and court supervision can make defective assessment consequential; the route need not depend on a willing volunteer alone.
An actual completion claim is materially stronger evidence than historical assessments reviewed, while remaining below independent technical verification.
challenges: The seven-day order is not an observed seven-day deletion time; do not derive duration from a later public confirmation.
The record is court-assisted enforcement, not proof every ODPC DPIA submission is a prior-approval gate.
Startup lens: legal adequacy, consent and deletion obligations must be designed before collecting irreversible identifiers. No startup-wide or community-wide preference is inferred.
One litigant's account cannot establish deletion of every backup, derivative or external copy, nor erase historical harm.
unknowns: Original judgment and later compliance ruling; ODPC verification report; technical deletion scope/method; dates of actual completion; current appeal/restart status.
No fresh ODPC reviewed-DPIA register or representative review-time distribution recovered.
routes.decisionTest: Obtain ODPC's court-filed verification and the corresponding compliance disposition; reconcile collection inventory and derivatives to the ordered scope before claiming technically verified completion.

scoreImplications.implication: Upgrade evidence maturity to reported completion, not independently verified success
scoreImplications.reason: Original litigant expressly reports full compliance; technical corroboration remains absent

scoreImplications.implication: Model court/litigant roles when using this precedent
scoreImplications.reason: The causal enforcement path is broader than controller-to-ODPC filing
All unlawfully collected data is a legal scope, not an independently verified affected-person count

routes.headline: GAID already contains concrete risk-based audit, rights and stop/modify assessments; the annex must prove additionality

newEvidence.claim: Re-read GAID: art.10(11) allows further information requests; art.10(13) allows a CAR certificate upon filing; art.10(14) normally requires UHL/EHL filing through a licensed DPCO. A certificate is therefore not, by itself, a demonstrated technical pass.

GAID art.28(4) requires accredited certified-DPO vetting, art.28(5) incorporates DPIA outcome into CAR, and art.28(6) provides a possible platform restriction for failure/refusal/negligence in conducting DPIA. Schedule 4 includes necessity/alternatives, stakeholder consultation, disparate effects, mitigation, and go-ahead/modify/stop choices with review frequency.

GAID art.35 provides conditional approval for interoperable privacy measures where Commission direction is required; application includes three use cases and disadvantages; art.35(5) says the Commission may approve within 30 days. AI deployment is expressly included. This is not automatic mutual recognition.
newEvidence.locator: pp.40–41 art.35(3)–(6), including apparent cross-reference typo to art.36 in (3)

newEvidence.claim: NDPC's own 10 July 2025 account cites a NGN766.2 million MultiChoice fine. It does not establish collection, technical remediation, or failure by the company's auditor.
newEvidence.locator: Main article paragraph beginning He pointed out the risks

supports: Regulator lens: a technical annex can populate an existing DPIA/CAR workflow and additional-information power.
Affected-community lens: existing template's alternatives, dignity and rights requirements provide stronger protection targets than leakage-only testing.
challenges: Novelty is weaker than the original generic-annex framing: risk-based techniques, DPIA outcomes and modify/stop dispositions are already in GAID.
Startup lens: a full AI-inventory programme could impose disproportionate compliance cost; match assessment depth to concrete risk and reuse the existing return.
Do not claim the MultiChoice case demonstrates a false audit: that causal fact was not verified in the recovered original source.
A 30-day discretionary IDPM provision and annual CAR deadline do not establish actual approval or test throughput.
unknowns: Actual accepted AI annex and held-out retest; selected obligated controller/DPCO; evaluator conflict management and hours/cost; completed IDPM approval; 2027-specific variations.
No independently verified false-CAR incidence or successful technical remediation rate.
routes.decisionTest: Take an obligated controller's actual CAR/DPIA and ask whether an independently seeded material failure changes its final assessment and is corrected on retest; compare cost and findings with its ordinary audit.

ideas.title: Small risk-based audit challenge with a rights-outcome test
ideas.proposal: Pilot one AI workflow in an actually CAR-obligated controller, using GAID's existing DPIA structure. Independently introduce authorised synthetic access/deletion faults in a staging copy and test whether the DPCO detects them, modifies the assessment and verifies correction.
ideas.owner: NDPC as regulatory interpretation/acceptance owner; a selected licensed DPCO as auditor; controller management as processing/remediation owner; accredited certified DPO vets the DPIA
ideas.mechanism: GAID arts.10(11), 28(4)–(6), Schedule 4; consider art.35 only if the imported protocol actually needs a specific Commission directive
ideas.safetyDemand: Evidence of lawful necessary processing, effective access/deletion rights and material-failure correction; no pass based solely on a certificate or AI policy
ideas.verification: Pre-register synthetic faults and independent scoring; retain the original audit conclusion, detected/missed issues, management decision, held-out retest, unresolved rights failures and staff-hours/cash cost. Test the subject-facing correction/deletion route as well as access controls.
ideas.remedy: Management corrects or stops the affected workflow; NDPC applies existing duties and procedures to actual legal breaches. Poor experimental performance alone is not a new statutory offence.
ideas.deadline: Proposed: eligible partner and staging authority by 2026-12-15; evidence ready for the applicable 2027 CAR deadline; retest by 2027-05-31. Verify entity-specific deadline, not a universal March assumption.
dependencies: CAR eligibility and applicable filing deadline
Staging environment, vendor rights and synthetic data

Potential adverse effects: audit gaming, fixed-cost burden on small firms, confidentiality leakage and disruption; cap the first workflow, separate remediation from independent retest and publish cost/error ranges rather than rankings
ideas.whyBetter: Measures whether existing obligations detect failures and change behaviour instead of adding another form or rewarding a filed certificate

scoreImplications.implication: Stronger workflow fit, weaker claimed novelty
scoreImplications.reason: Existing law/template already incorporates risk-based audit, DPIA and action choices

scoreImplications.implication: Separate certification, legal consequences and observed correction
scoreImplications.reason: Certificate may follow filing; actual successful fault detection and correction remain unobserved

routes.headline: Rights-facing duties broaden the test target, but no implementation case was recovered

newEvidence.claim: Re-read official law text: art.37 requires rectification/erasure of inaccurate data without delay; art.42 includes notice of automated decision-making logic, significance and envisaged consequences and the right to appeal; art.45 addresses high-risk breach communication to data subjects, subject to stated exceptions.

The official compliance-tools page links a DPIA guide/form, inventory checklist, complaint guide and MSME guide. The DPIA PDF body remained unread after unsupported-PDF and connection-timeout attempts; existence of a link is not proof of its contents or use.
newEvidence.locator: Compliance Tools document list; direct PDF access attempts

supports: Affected-community lens: a proposed retest can include whether people receive intelligible explanations and can correct errors, rather than security tests alone.
Regulator lens: the existing data-controller duties supply specific obligations to which failures would need to be tied.
challenges: No recovered booked case, staffed review team or actual successful retest supports upgrading operational readiness.
Startup lens: the presence of an MSME guide is a lead for proportionate support, not evidence that small firms find compliance affordable or that exemptions apply.
The wider rights duties do not establish a blanket prior-authorisation requirement or an automated-decision veto.
unknowns: DPIA guide body, review register and measured turnaround; named eligible workflow; accepted test and remedy; actual technical capacity and affected-user outcomes.
routes.decisionTest: Obtain a completed in-scope DPIA and supervisory disposition; reproduce one security or erroneous-profile defect and verify the user can obtain correction under the applicable duty.
